title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with default Study mode and age routing
subtitle: Users 13–17 now get a distinct experience with study-focused prompts, restricted romantic language, and parental controls — the first age-gated default from a frontier lab.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens on August 18, 2026 — a distinct default experience for users aged 13 to 17. The teen product ships with a study-focused starting screen, ChatGPT's Study mode enabled by default, and 'Study hours' that let a teen or a linked parent choose windows in which new chats open in study mode. Teen accounts receive additional content protections around self-harm, eating disorders, violence, dangerous activities, and sexual or graphic content. OpenAI also said the model will not use romantic language or terms of endearment with teen accounts and will be instructed more strongly to state that it is an AI without feelings or consciousness.

The launch follows a run of legal and regulatory pressure — including wrongful-death suits filed by parents of teenagers who used ChatGPT in 2025 and 2026, and the FTC comment window on AI accuracy that closed in July. Age prediction routes minor users into the teen experience automatically; parental linking is optional but unlocks the study-hour controls and a summary view. OpenAI positions the product as a 'default' for that age band rather than a niche mode, a notable shift from earlier framings that treated safety features as opt-in.

The launch also lands into a fuller regulatory calendar than any previous OpenAI teen effort. California's AI Transparency Act takes effect this month, Illinois's AI Safety Measures Act was signed in July, and the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations became enforceable on August 2. OpenAI's teen product is unlikely to satisfy every jurisdiction — parental-controls schemes are notoriously easy for teens to work around — but it is the first frontier lab to ship an age-gated default rather than a checkbox setting. Anthropic launched Claude for Teachers in July, though that product addressed educators rather than students directly.

For teachers and parents, the practical takeaway is narrower than the announcement suggests. Study mode is a scaffolding layer, not a truth filter — the model can still hallucinate a citation or confidently misexplain a concept whether or not it's addressing a 15-year-old. What the teen product actually reduces is a specific class of harm (grooming-style dialogue, sycophancy) and it adds friction on another (endless late-night chat as substitute for sleep). Everything a student learns from it still needs a second source.
